title: Testing & TypeScript
intro: Senior engineers are expected to ship code that is safe to change. Interviewers ask about testing to see whether you can get real confidence quickly, without slow, flaky or over-mocked suites, and about TypeScript to see whether you use the type system to prevent bugs while remembering that types vanish at runtime.

questions.title: Unit vs integration vs e2e
questions.question: How do you split unit, integration and end-to-end tests for a Node API?
questions.short: Unit tests check one function or class in isolation, with no network or database, so they are fast and pinpoint bugs in business logic. Integration tests run real pieces together, typically the HTTP layer plus a real database in a container, and catch wiring, SQL and serialization bugs. End-to-end tests hit the deployed system like a client would and are few, slow and focused on critical flows. For APIs I lean heavily on integration tests through HTTP, because that is where most real bugs live, with unit tests for complex logic.
questions.simple: Unit tests check each brick. Integration tests check that the bricks hold together as a wall. End-to-end tests walk through the finished house.

head: Unit
Integration
End-to-end
rows: Sign up, pay and get email in staging

explain.h: A practical shape for Node APIs

list: Unit: pure functions such as pricing rules, parsers, permission checks. No mocks needed if the code is pure.
Integration: most tests. Start the app in-process, send real HTTP with supertest, use a real database from Testcontainers or docker compose, and stub only third-party HTTP.
Contract tests at the edges with external APIs, if you have many consumers.
E2E: a handful of smoke tests on the main user journeys after deploy.

explain.h: Design the code so it is testable

explain.note: Tests that mock everything often pass while production breaks. A senior answer is about confidence per minute of test time, not coverage percentage.

followups.q: What is the testing pyramid vs the testing trophy?
followups.a: The pyramid says many unit tests, fewer integration, very few e2e. The trophy (popular for web apps) puts integration tests as the biggest layer because they give the most confidence per cost. For CRUD-heavy APIs the trophy is often a better fit.

followups.q: Is 100% coverage a good goal?
followups.a: No. Coverage shows what was executed, not what was checked. Aim for good coverage of important logic and error paths, and look at mutation testing if you want to measure test quality.

mistakes: Calling a test with a mocked database an integration test.
Having only e2e tests, which are slow and flaky.
Exporting an app that already calls listen(), making in-process tests hard.

questions.title: Jest, Vitest and node:test
questions.question: Which test runner would you use for a Node service: Jest, Vitest or the built-in node:test?
questions.short: Jest is the long-time standard with a huge ecosystem, but native ESM support is still experimental and TypeScript needs a transform. Vitest has a Jest-compatible API, handles ESM and TypeScript out of the box and is fast, so it is my default for new TypeScript projects. The built-in `node:test` runner (stable since Node 20) needs no dependencies and has describe/it, mocks, fake timers and coverage, which makes it great for libraries and smaller services where you want zero tooling.
questions.simple: Jest is the big, well-known toolbox. Vitest is a newer, faster toolbox that fits modern parts. node:test is the screwdriver that comes free with Node.

head: Jest
Vitest
node:test
rows: Via type stripping or a loader like tsx
Separate worker or process per file by default

explain.code:
node --test                        # finds *.test.js and friends
node --test --watch
node --test --experimental-test-coverage

explain.note: Whatever runner you choose, run tests in CI with the same Node version as production.

followups.q: Why do tests run in separate processes or workers?
followups.a: So that module state, globals and mocks from one file cannot leak into another, and files can run in parallel. The cost is start-up time per file.

followups.q: How do you run a single test?
followups.a: Jest/Vitest: `it.only` or a name filter (`-t "name"`). node:test: `--test-name-pattern="name"`, or `it.only` with `--test-only`.

mistakes: Picking Jest for a pure-ESM TypeScript project and fighting configuration.
Not knowing Node has a built-in test runner.
Leaving `.only` in committed code (use a lint rule to forbid it).

questions.title: Mocking modules and HTTP
questions.question: How do you mock dependencies in Node tests, including outgoing HTTP calls? When should you not mock?
questions.short: I prefer dependency injection: pass a fake object in and avoid module mocking. When needed, `jest.mock` or `vi.mock` replace whole modules, and spies like `vi.spyOn` replace one method. For outgoing HTTP I mock at the network layer with nock or msw, so my real HTTP client code still runs and I assert on the request. I do not mock what I own and can run cheaply, like my own database layer in integration tests, or the code under test itself; heavy mocking tests the mocks, not the system.
questions.simple: Mocking is using a cardboard cut-out of a person in a rehearsal. Great for actors you cannot book, but if the whole cast is cardboard, you learn nothing about the show.

head: Technique
Example
Good for
rows: Most cases. No magic, works in any runner.
Checking a call happened, forcing an error
Code that imports a module directly
Third-party APIs, keeps your client code real

explain.p: msw intercepts `fetch` and the `http` module. nock works by intercepting the `http` module; versions before nock 14 do not see the built-in `fetch`. Undici's `MockAgent` is another option for fetch. Setting unhandled requests to error makes sure no test calls the real internet.

list: Your own database queries: use a real database in integration tests. Mocked SQL never catches a wrong column name.
Simple pure functions your code calls: just let them run.
Everything around the unit under test, so the test only checks that mocks were called in a certain order.
Libraries you do not control in the exact way they behave (for example how pg returns numbers); mocking them encodes your assumptions, not reality.

explain.note: Reset or restore mocks between tests (`vi.restoreAllMocks()`, `mock.restoreAll()`), or enable `restoreMocks` in config, so state does not leak.

anim.title: nock intercepts an outgoing request

steps.note: Importing nock patches Node's http and https request functions so it can see outgoing requests.
We register an interceptor: a GET to api.github.com/users/ana will get a fake 200 reply.
Our real getUser code runs, builds the URL and sends the request with its real HTTP client.
nock matches the request against the interceptor. No packet leaves the machine.
The fake JSON body flows back through the real response parsing and mapping code.
We assert on the mapped result: our code turned login into name and public_repos into repos.
isDone() confirms every interceptor was used, so the code really made the call we expected.

followups.q: What is the difference between a mock, a stub and a spy?
followups.a: A stub returns canned answers. A spy records calls, optionally wrapping the real function. A mock is a fake with expectations you assert on. Test libraries often use one function (vi.fn, jest.fn) for all three.

followups.q: How do you make sure tests never call real third-party APIs?
followups.a: Use msw with onUnhandledRequest: "error", or `nock.disableNetConnect()` with `nock.enableNetConnect("127.0.0.1")` for local test servers.

followups.q: Why are module mocks hoisted?
followups.a: vi.mock and jest.mock calls are moved to the top of the file so the mock is registered before the imports load the real module.

mistakes: Mocking the database in tests that are supposed to check SQL.
Forgetting to restore spies, so one test changes another.
Using nock with an old version and native fetch, then wondering why requests are not intercepted.
Asserting only that mocks were called, never on real outputs.

questions.title: Fake timers
questions.question: How do you test code with setTimeout, retries with backoff or TTL caches without making the test slow?
questions.short: I use fake timers, which replace setTimeout, setInterval and usually Date with a virtual clock. The test then moves time forward manually with `vi.advanceTimersByTime`, `jest.advanceTimersByTime` or `mock.timers.tick` in node:test, so a 30-second backoff runs in microseconds and the test is deterministic. With promises in the mix I use the async variants like `advanceTimersByTimeAsync`, so promise callbacks get a chance to run between timers.
questions.simple: Fake timers give the test a remote control for the clock: instead of waiting 30 seconds, you press fast forward exactly 30 seconds.

explain.p: The async version matters: the retry code awaits a rejected promise before it schedules the next timer. `advanceTimersByTimeAsync` flushes those promise callbacks between timer steps; the sync version may advance the clock before the next timer even exists.

list: Always restore real timers after the test, or other tests and libraries break.
Fake timers do not speed up real I/O. A real DB query still takes real time.
Some libraries capture `setTimeout` when they load; enable fake timers before importing them, or inject a clock.
If code uses `Date.now()` for expiry, fake `Date` too, not just timers.
`mock.timers` in node:test is still marked experimental in Node 20 and 22.

explain.note: Injecting a clock (`{ now: () => Date.now() }`) is often simpler and more explicit than global fake timers.

anim.title: Advancing a fake clock

steps.note: enable() swaps the global setTimeout for a fake one. The fake clock starts at 0 and only moves when we tell it to.
The callback is stored in the fake timer list, due at 1000ms. Nothing is given to the real event loop.
Synchronous log.
tick(999) moves the clock to 999ms instantly. The timer is not due yet, so nothing fires.
No real time passed. This proves the boundary: 1ms early is still too early.
tick(1) reaches 1000ms. The due callback runs synchronously, inside tick().
Back in main after tick returns. The whole test took microseconds instead of a second.
reset() restores the real setTimeout so other code is not affected.

followups.q: What is the difference between runAllTimers and advanceTimersByTime?
followups.a: runAllTimers runs every pending timer, including ones scheduled by those timers, until none are left (and can loop forever with setInterval). advanceTimersByTime moves a precise amount, which is usually what you want.

followups.q: Why does my test hang with fake timers?
followups.a: Often the code awaits a promise that only resolves after a timer, but the test awaits that promise before advancing the clock. Start the operation, advance timers, then await the result.

mistakes: Using real sleeps like `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, 2000))` in tests.
Advancing timers synchronously when the code awaits between timers.
Forgetting to restore real timers.

questions.title: Testing an Express API with supertest
questions.question: How do you test Express routes end to end inside the test process?
questions.short: I export a function that builds the Express app without calling listen, then pass the app to supertest. supertest starts it on an ephemeral port, sends a real HTTP request, and lets me assert on status, headers and body. The full middleware chain runs: JSON parsing, auth, validation, the handler and the error handler, so it catches wiring bugs that unit tests miss. I combine it with a real test database and fake only third-party services.
questions.simple: supertest is a robot client that knocks on your app's door from inside the same building, without you having to open the shop to the street.

list: The happy path with the exact response shape.
Validation errors (400) and their messages.
Auth (401) and permissions (403).
Not found (404) and conflicts (409, for example a duplicate email from a unique index).
That the database really changed, by querying it after the request.

explain.code:
const token = signTestJwt({ sub: 'user-1', role: 'admin' });
await request(app).get('/admin/stats').set('authorization', `Bearer ${token}`).expect(200);

explain.note: Passing `app` (not a running server) means each request gets an ephemeral port and the server is closed afterwards, so there are no port conflicts when tests run in parallel. If you pass a server you started yourself, close it in afterAll.

anim.title: One supertest request through the app

steps.note: We build the app with the test database injected. It is not listening on any port yet.
request(app) starts the app on a random free port, only for this request.
The request is described: method, path, JSON body. Awaiting it sends a real HTTP request over the loopback.
Express runs the chain in order. First express.json parses the body into req.body.
Validation passes, so the handler runs and inserts a row into the real test database.
The handler responds 201 with JSON. supertest checks the status; a mismatch would fail with a clear message.
We assert on the parsed body. The test covered parsing, validation, SQL and serialization in one go.

followups.q: Does supertest work with Fastify?
followups.a: It works with any Node http server, but Fastify has a built-in `app.inject()` that simulates requests without opening a socket at all, which is faster and the recommended way.

followups.q: How do you avoid test data clashes between tests?
followups.a: Use unique values per test (random emails), wrap each test in a rolled-back transaction, or truncate tables between tests. Run files in parallel only if each has its own schema or database.

mistakes: Importing a module that already calls app.listen(3000), causing EADDRINUSE in parallel tests.
Only testing the happy path.
Forgetting to close DB pools, so the test runner never exits.

questions.title: Testing async code and rejections
questions.question: How do you test async functions and make sure a promise rejects with the right error?
questions.short: Make the test function async and `await` everything. For rejections use `await expect(fn()).rejects.toThrow(...)` in Jest/Vitest or `await assert.rejects(promise, matcher)` with node:assert. The most common bug is forgetting `await` or `return` on the assertion: the test finishes and passes before the promise settles, and the failure shows up later or not at all.
questions.simple: If you do not wait for the answer, you leave the exam room before the teacher grades you and assume you passed.

list: Callbacks: wrap with `util.promisify` or `new Promise`, or use the `done` callback (avoid mixing it with async functions).
Events: `const [msg] = await events.once(emitter, "message")`.
Streams: `await pipeline(...)` or collect with `for await`.
Background work started by the code (fire-and-forget): expose a promise or a hook to await, otherwise the test cannot know when it finished.

explain.note: Turn on the `@typescript-eslint/no-floating-promises` or `vitest/valid-expect` lint rules: they catch most missing awaits automatically.

anim.title: A missing await makes a failing check look green

steps.note: main() starts. Think of it as an async test body.
findUser(1) resolves with { id: 1 }. await pauses main until the value is ready, then deepEqual checks it.
The happy-path check passed.
findUser(-1) rejects. assert.rejects awaits it and checks the error message against /invalid id/. It matches, so the assertion promise resolves.
Because we awaited, this line runs only after the check really finished.
Bug: no await. findUser(1) resolves, which should FAIL the rejects check, but that check needs a few microtasks to finish.
main keeps going immediately. In a test runner, the test body would end here and be reported as passed.
We attach a catch only so the demo prints instead of crashing.
Microtasks run: assert.rejects sees that the promise resolved and rejects p with an AssertionError.
The failure arrives after the "test" already ended. In a real runner it becomes an unhandled rejection or is blamed on a different test.

followups.q: What does expect.assertions(n) do?
followups.a: It makes the test fail unless exactly n assertions ran. Useful when assertions live in callbacks or catch blocks that might never run.

followups.q: How do you test that something does NOT throw?
followups.a: Just await it: `await expect(fn()).resolves.toBeDefined()` or simply `await fn()`; a rejection fails the test.

mistakes: Forgetting await on expect(...).rejects or assert.rejects.
Writing try/catch tests that pass when nothing throws.
Passing the function result to toThrow (sync matcher) instead of using rejects for promises.

questions.title: Test database strategies
questions.question: How do you run tests against a real database and keep them isolated and fast?
questions.short: I start a real database of the same engine and version as production, usually with Testcontainers or docker compose in CI, and run migrations once at the start. For isolation I wrap each test in a transaction and roll it back at the end, or truncate tables between tests when the code under test manages its own transactions. For parallel test files, each worker gets its own database or schema. I avoid SQLite or in-memory fakes for a Postgres app because SQL dialects and constraints differ.
questions.simple: Each test borrows a whiteboard, writes on it, and then the whiteboard is wiped clean before the next test, so nobody sees someone else's notes.

head: Strategy
How
Pros
Cons
rows: BEGIN before each test, ROLLBACK after
Code must use the same connection; breaks if code commits or opens its own transactions
`TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE` after each test
Data piles up; count-based assertions get harder

list: Savepoints let code that uses its own nested transactions still work inside the test transaction.
Seed reference data (countries, plans) once after migrations, not per test.
Use factories (`makeUser({ role: "admin" })`) instead of large shared fixture files.

explain.note: Testcontainers needs Docker on the machine. In CI, either enable Docker or use the CI service containers feature with the same image version.

anim.title: Each test runs inside a transaction that is rolled back

steps.note: Before the test, the database holds only seed data that was committed after migrations.
beforeEach takes one connection from the pool for this test.
BEGIN opens a transaction on that connection. Everything the test writes will be invisible to others until commit.
The repository is built with the same client, so its queries run inside our transaction.
The insert happens inside the transaction. It is visible on conn1 only.
count() on the same connection sees its own uncommitted row, so the assertion passes.
afterEach rolls back. The order row disappears as if it never existed. No cleanup scripts needed.
The connection goes back to the pool. The next test starts from exactly the same data.

followups.q: Why not use SQLite in memory for tests?
followups.a: It is a different engine: different SQL features, types, locking and constraint behaviour. Tests can pass on SQLite and fail on Postgres. Containers make the real engine cheap enough.

followups.q: How do you test code that commits its own transactions?
followups.a: Truncate tables between tests, or use a fresh database per test file created from a template database, which Postgres can copy quickly.

mistakes: Sharing one database between parallel test files without isolation, causing flaky tests.
Using transaction rollback while the code under test grabs a different pool connection, so its writes are committed and leak.
Running migrations before every test instead of once.

questions.title: TypeScript: strict, type vs interface, unknown
questions.question: What tsconfig settings matter for a Node backend? When do you use type vs interface, and unknown vs any?
questions.short: I always enable `strict`, which turns on `strictNullChecks`, `noImplicitAny` and friends, and I often add `noUncheckedIndexedAccess`. For Node I set `module` and `moduleResolution` to `nodenext` (or `node16`) so TypeScript follows Node's real ESM/CJS rules. Interfaces and type aliases mostly overlap for object shapes; interfaces can be extended and merged, while types can express unions, intersections and mapped types, so I use types for unions and either one consistently for objects. `any` turns off checking; `unknown` means "could be anything, prove it before use", so external data like JSON or caught errors should be `unknown`.
questions.simple: any is a "skip the security check" pass. unknown is a sealed package: you can hold it, but you must open and inspect it before using what is inside.

explain.code:
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "target": "ES2023",
    "module": "nodenext",
    "moduleResolution": "nodenext",
    "strict": true,
    "noUncheckedIndexedAccess": true,
    "exactOptionalPropertyTypes": true,
    "verbatimModuleSyntax": true,
    "skipLibCheck": true,
    "outDir": "dist",
    "rootDir": "src",
    "sourceMap": true
  },
  "include": ["src"]
}

list: `strict`: catches null/undefined bugs, implicit any and unsafe `this`.
`noUncheckedIndexedAccess`: `arr[0]` and `record[key]` become `T | undefined`, which matches reality.
`nodenext`: requires `.js` extensions in relative ESM imports, respects `"type"` and `"exports"`.
`verbatimModuleSyntax`: forces `import type` for type-only imports, which also keeps code compatible with type stripping.

explain.note: `any` spreads: anything you get from an `any` value is also `any`. One `any` at a boundary can silently disable checking across many files.

followups.q: What does `as` do at runtime?
followups.a: Nothing. A type assertion only tells the compiler to trust you; if you are wrong, you get a runtime error later. Validate external data instead of asserting.

followups.q: What is `satisfies`?
followups.a: It checks that a value matches a type without widening it to that type, so you keep the precise inferred type. Handy for config objects: `const routes = {...} satisfies Record<string, Route>`.

followups.q: What is a discriminated union?
followups.a: A union where every member has a common literal field, like `ok: true | false` or `type: "card" | "bank"`. Checking that field narrows to the exact member, and a `never` check in a switch catches unhandled cases.

mistakes: Turning off strict to "move faster".
Using any for JSON from requests or third-party APIs.
Using `as` casts instead of validation at boundaries.
Using module: commonjs settings while running the code as ESM, causing import errors at runtime.

questions.title: Generics and typing Express
questions.question: Show a practical use of generics in a Node backend, and explain how you type Express request and response objects.
questions.short: Generics let one function or type work with many types while keeping them connected, for example a `paginate<T>()` helper or a repository `findById<T>()` that returns the right entity type. For Express, `Request` and `Response` are generic: `Request<Params, ResBody, ReqBody, Query>` and `Response<ResBody>`, so handlers can type params, body and response. Extra properties like `req.user` are added with declaration merging on `Express.Request`. Types are only compile-time, so the body still needs runtime validation.
questions.simple: A generic is a labelled box with a blank label. When you use it, you fill in the label, and TypeScript makes sure only matching things go in and come out.

explain.p: The constraint `T extends { id: string }` lets the function read `.id` while still returning the caller's exact type, not a vague base type.

list: This is interface declaration merging: it adds a field to Express's own Request type everywhere.
Make it optional unless every route is behind auth, then narrow after the auth middleware.
The `Body` generic is a promise you make to the compiler, not a check. Validate `req.body` with Zod at runtime and use the inferred type.

explain.note: Express 4 does not catch rejected promises from async handlers; you need a wrapper or express-async-errors. Express 5 forwards rejections to the error handler automatically.

followups.q: What is the difference between `<T>` and `<T extends X>`?
followups.a: A bare T can be anything, so you can do almost nothing with it inside the function. extends adds a constraint, so you can use X's properties while still returning the specific type.

followups.q: Name some built-in generic utility types.
followups.a: `Partial<T>`, `Required<T>`, `Pick<T, K>`, `Omit<T, K>`, `Record<K, V>`, `ReturnType<F>`, `Awaited<T>`, `NonNullable<T>`.

mistakes: Typing req.body as a DTO and trusting it without validation.
Writing `function get(): any` repositories, losing all type safety at the data layer.
Adding generics that are only used once, which adds noise without safety.

questions.title: Running TypeScript in Node
questions.question: How do you run a TypeScript Node service in development and in production?
questions.short: In production I compile with `tsc` to JavaScript in a build step and run plain `node dist/server.js`, which gives the fastest startup and no extra runtime tools. In development I use a fast runner like tsx (esbuild-based) or ts-node, often with watch mode, and run `tsc --noEmit` separately in CI for type checking, because these runners do not type-check. Newer Node can also run .ts files directly by stripping types: on by default in Node 23.6+ and 22.18+, with a flag on earlier 22.x; it only handles erasable syntax and never type-checks.
questions.simple: TypeScript is like a draft with teacher's notes. Before the show you print a clean copy (tsc). In rehearsal you can read the draft directly and just ignore the notes (tsx or type stripping).

head: Tool
Type-checks?
How
Good for
rows: Yes by default (slow); can be turned off
Removes type annotations, runs the result

list: Added in Node 22.6 behind `--experimental-strip-types`; enabled by default in Node 23.6 and backported to 22.18.

Only "erasable" syntax: type annotations, interfaces, type aliases, `import type`. Enums, namespaces with values, and constructor parameter properties need `--experimental-transform-types` or a different tool.
It does not read tsconfig.json and does not do path aliases.
Imports must use the real `.ts` extension, and type-only imports should use `import type`. The TS option `erasableSyntaxOnly` (TS 5.8+) helps enforce this.
Files inside node_modules are not stripped, so libraries still need to publish JavaScript.

explain.code:
node src/server.ts                         # Node 23.6+ / 22.18+
node --experimental-strip-types src/server.ts   # Node 22.6 - 22.17

list: Use a multi-stage Docker build: compile in a stage with devDependencies, copy only `dist` and production `node_modules` into the final image.
Ship source maps and run with `--enable-source-maps` so stack traces point at .ts lines.
Keep type checking in CI as a separate step; a fast runner passing does not mean the types are correct.

explain.note: Path aliases like `@/utils` are resolved by tsc for types but not rewritten in output. Prefer package.json `"imports"` (`#utils`), which Node understands natively.

followups.q: Why not run tsx in production?
followups.a: It works, but you pay the transform cost at startup, add a dependency to the runtime image and lose a clear build artifact. Compiled JS is simpler to debug and to scan.

followups.q: What about bundling a Node service with esbuild?
followups.a: It is a valid option for fast cold starts (for example serverless): one file, fewer node_modules. Watch out for native modules and dynamic requires, which must stay external.

mistakes: Assuming tsx or type stripping catches type errors.
Using enums or parameter properties and expecting native type stripping to run them.
Shipping TypeScript and the compiler into the production image without need.

questions.title: Runtime validation with Zod
questions.question: TypeScript types disappear at runtime. How do you make sure request bodies and env variables actually match your types?
questions.short: I validate at every boundary: request bodies, query params, env variables, third-party API responses and queue messages. With Zod I define a schema once, validate with `safeParse` (or `parse`, which throws), and derive the static type with `z.infer<typeof Schema>`, so the runtime check and the TypeScript type can never drift apart. On failure I return a 400 with the issues; on success I get typed, cleaned data, since unknown keys are stripped by default.
questions.simple: TypeScript is the guest list printed at home. Zod is the bouncer at the door who actually checks IDs, and the guest list is generated from the bouncer's rules.

list: Validate at the edges, then trust the types inside.
Use `.strict()` on objects when unknown keys should be an error instead of silently stripped.
Do not return raw validation internals to clients if they reveal too much; map issues to path + message.
Alternatives: Valibot, TypeBox (JSON Schema, works well with Fastify), ArkType. The idea is the same.

explain.note: `parse` throws a ZodError; `safeParse` returns `{ success, data | error }`. Use `parseAsync`/`safeParseAsync` if the schema has async refinements.

anim.title: safeParse turns unknown input into typed data

steps.note: The schema is a normal runtime object. It exists in the compiled JavaScript, unlike a TypeScript interface.
z.infer builds the static type from the schema at compile time. No duplicate interface to keep in sync.
Request 1 arrives. The body is just parsed JSON: TypeScript knows nothing about it.
email passes. age is the string 30; coerce turns it into the number 30, which passes int and min(18).
success is true. data has the right types, and the unknown key isAdmin was stripped, which blocks mass-assignment tricks.
Request 2: a bad email and age 15.
Zod does not stop at the first problem. It collects every issue with its path.
success is false, so we answer 400 with the issue list. The handler code below never sees invalid data.

followups.q: Why not just use TypeScript types for the body?
followups.a: Types are erased at compile time. A client can send anything; without a runtime check, a string where you expect a number flows straight into your SQL or business logic.

followups.q: How do you share schemas with the frontend?
followups.a: Put them in a shared package in a monorepo, or generate an OpenAPI spec from them (for example with zod-openapi libraries) and generate client types from that.

mistakes: Writing an interface and a separate validation schema by hand, so they drift.
Validating only the request body, not query params, env variables or third-party responses.
Using parse in a handler without catching the ZodError, turning bad input into a 500.
